claim: Keratinocytes are the most abundant cell type in the epidermis.
source: Keratinocytes are the most abundant cell type in the epidermis, the most superficial layer of skin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental support in this manuscript.

claim: Keratinocytes are critical for normal mechanotransduction and mechanically-evoked behavioral responses in mice.
source: recent work from our lab (Moehring et al., 2018) and others (Baumbauer et al., 2015) has demonstrated that keratinocytes are also critical for normal mechanotransduction and mechanically-evoked behavioral responses in mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Keratinocyte cold activity is conserved across mammalian species.
source: Using calcium imaging, we determined that keratinocyte cold activity is conserved across mammalian species and requires the release of intracellular calcium through one or more unknown cold-sensitive proteins.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments performed on keratinocytes from multiple mammalian species as described in the manuscript.

claim: Keratinocyte cold responses require the release of intracellular calcium through one or more unknown cold-sensitive proteins.
source: Using calcium imaging, we determined that keratinocyte cold activity is conserved across mammalian species and requires the release of intracellular calcium through one or more unknown cold-sensitive proteins.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments with various pharmacological manipulations described in the manuscript.

claim: Epidermal cell optogenetic inhibition reduces reflexive behavioral responses to cold stimuli.
source: Both epidermal cell optogenetic inhibition and interruption of ATP-P2X4 signaling reduced reflexive behavioral responses to cold and heat stimuli.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments using optogenetic inhibition in Krt14:Arch mice.

claim: Interruption of ATP-P2X4 signaling reduces reflexive behavioral responses to cold stimuli.
source: Both epidermal cell optogenetic inhibition and interruption of ATP-P2X4 signaling reduced reflexive behavioral responses to cold and heat stimuli.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments using apyrase treatment and P2X4 knockout mice.

claim: Epidermal cell optogenetic inhibition reduces reflexive behavioral responses to heat stimuli.
source: Both epidermal cell optogenetic inhibition and interruption of ATP-P2X4 signaling reduced reflexive behavioral responses to cold and heat stimuli.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments using optogenetic inhibition in Krt14:Arch mice.

claim: Interruption of ATP-P2X4 signaling reduces reflexive behavioral responses to heat stimuli.
source: Both epidermal cell optogenetic inhibition and interruption of ATP-P2X4 signaling reduced reflexive behavioral responses to cold and heat stimuli.
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments using apyrase treatment and P2X4 knockout mice.

claim: Keratinocyte purinergic signaling is a modality-conserved amplification system required for normal somatosensation in vivo.
source: Based on these data and our previous findings, keratinocyte purinergic signaling is a modality-conserved amplification system that is required for normal somatosensation in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current experimental data and previous findings cited in the manuscript.

claim: Keratinocytes constitute 95% of the epidermis.
source: These specialized epidermal cells have received significantly more attention in somatosensory research than keratinocytes, the so-called 'barrier cells' that constitute 95% of the epidermis.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge without specific citation in this manuscript.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of keratin14-expressing cells decreases mechanically-induced firing in Aβ, Aδ, and C fiber afferents.
source: optogenetic inhibition of keratin14-expressing cells decreases mechanically-induced firing in Aβ, Aδ, and C fiber afferents (Baumbauer et al., 2015) and behavioral responses to hindpaw mechanical stimulation in naïve mice (Moehring et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of keratin14-expressing cells decreases behavioral responses to hindpaw mechanical stimulation in naïve mice.
source: optogenetic inhibition of keratin14-expressing cells decreases mechanically-induced firing in Aβ, Aδ, and C fiber afferents (Baumbauer et al., 2015) and behavioral responses to hindpaw mechanical stimulation in naïve mice (Moehring et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Primary keratinocytes from both mouse and human exhibit cold-induced calcium transients.
source: Primary keratinocytes from both mouse and human exhibit cold-induced calcium transients (Bidaux et al., 2015; Tsutsumi et al., 2010), but a direct comparison of these responses has not yet been performed.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: A direct comparison of cold-induced calcium transients in mouse and human keratinocytes has not yet been performed.
source: Primary keratinocytes from both mouse and human exhibit cold-induced calcium transients (Bidaux et al., 2015; Tsutsumi et al., 2010), but a direct comparison of these responses has not yet been performed.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to this study.

claim: Over 92% of mouse keratinocytes responded to decreasing temperatures.
source: Over 92% of mouse keratinocytes responded to decreasing temperatures (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The magnitude of the peak cold response in mouse keratinocytes was a 56% increase from baseline.
source: On average, the magnitude of the peak cold response was a 56% increase from baseline (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Cold-induced transients in mouse keratinocytes were initiated when the buffer temperature dropped below 20.9°C.
source: cold-induced transients were initiated when the buffer temperature dropped below 20.9°C (a 3°C drop from the starting temperature; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Only 47% of rat keratinocytes exhibited cold-induced calcium transients.
source: Only 47% of rat keratinocytes exhibited cold-induced calcium transients, the peak magnitudes and temperature thresholds of which were lower than mouse (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The peak magnitudes and temperature thresholds of rat keratinocyte cold responses were lower than mouse.
source: Only 47% of rat keratinocytes exhibited cold-induced calcium transients, the peak magnitudes and temperature thresholds of which were lower than mouse (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Mus musculus and Rattus norvegicus are members of the Muridae family that inhabit similar climates.
source: Mus musculus and Rattus novegicus are members of the Muridae family that inhabit similar climates (Feng and Himsworth, 2014; Latham and Mason, 2004) and maintain similar core and skin temperatures.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Mus musculus and Rattus norvegicus maintain similar core and skin temperatures.
source: Mus musculus and Rattus novegicus are members of the Muridae family that inhabit similar climates (Feng and Himsworth, 2014; Latham and Mason, 2004) and maintain similar core and skin temperatures.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, though not directly cited.

claim: Both mouse and rat species exhibit similar reflexive and thermotactic behaviors when exposed to cold stimuli or environments.
source: Both species exhibit similar reflexive and thermotactic behaviors when exposed to cold stimuli or environments, and ex vivo skin-nerve recordings have identified spontaneously active, low-threshold cool fibers and quiescent, high-threshold cold fibers (Leem et al., 1993; Koltzenburg et al., 1997; Paricio-Montesinos et al., 2020) in both species.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, though not directly cited for the behavioral claim.

claim: Ex vivo skin-nerve recordings have identified spontaneously active, low-threshold cool fibers and quiescent, high-threshold cold fibers in both mouse and rat.
source: Both species exhibit similar reflexive and thermotactic behaviors when exposed to cold stimuli or environments, and ex vivo skin-nerve recordings have identified spontaneously active, low-threshold cool fibers and quiescent, high-threshold cold fibers (Leem et al., 1993; Koltzenburg et al., 1997; Paricio-Montesinos et al., 2020) in both species.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Over 96% of squirrel keratinocytes responded to decreasing temperatures.
source: Over 96% of squirrel keratinocytes responded to decreasing temperatures (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Cold-induced calcium transients in squirrel keratinocytes were larger than those observed in mouse or rat.
source: Cold-induced calcium transients in squirrel keratinocytes were larger than those observed in mouse or rat and were initiated at a threshold of ~19°C (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Cold-induced calcium transients in squirrel keratinocytes were initiated at a threshold of ~19°C.
source: Cold-induced calcium transients in squirrel keratinocytes were larger than those observed in mouse or rat and were initiated at a threshold of ~19°C (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: 13-lined ground squirrels are less sensitive to innocuous and noxious cold than mice as a result of amino acid substitutions in the TRPM8 channel and decreased cold-sensitivity of dorsal root ganglia neurons.
source: In laboratory behavioral studies, these rodents are less sensitive to innocuous and noxious cold than mice as a result of amino acid substitutions in the TRPM8 channel and decreased cold-sensitivity of dorsal root ganglia neurons (Matos-Cruz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Suppressed cold sensation is proposed to be metabolically advantageous for species that spend extended periods of time in hibernation.
source: Suppressed cold sensation is proposed to be metabolically advantageous for species that spend extended periods of time in hibernation (Matos-Cruz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Upon warming, keratinocytes release ATP that subsequently activates nearby keratinocytes and/or sensory neurons via P2X receptor signaling.
source: Upon warming, keratinocytes release ATP that subsequently activates nearby keratinocytes and/or sensory neurons via P2X receptor signaling (Mandadi et al., 2009; Moehring et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Over 67% of human keratinocytes responded to decreasing temperatures.
source: Over 67% of human keratinocytes responded to decreasing temperatures (Figure 1B);>50% of the keratinocytes from each of the five tissue donors were cold sensitive (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: >50% of the keratinocytes from each of the five human tissue donors were cold sensitive.
source: Over 67% of human keratinocytes responded to decreasing temperatures (Figure 1B);>50% of the keratinocytes from each of the five tissue donors were cold sensitive (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 60% of undifferentiated human keratinocytes responded to cold in a previous report.
source: These results are similar to a previous report in which 60% of undifferentiated human keratinocytes responded to cold (Tsutsumi et al., 2010) (~24–12°C ramp).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Human keratinocytes were more responsive to cold than rat keratinocytes, exhibiting larger cold-induced calcium transients that were initiated at higher temperatures.
source: Human keratinocytes were more responsive to cold than rat keratinocytes, exhibiting larger cold-induced calcium transients that were initiated at higher temperatures.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Human keratinocytes were less responsive to cold than squirrel keratinocytes; a higher percentage of squirrel keratinocytes responded to cold with larger calcium transients.
source: Similarly, human keratinocytes were less responsive to cold than squirrel keratinocytes; a higher percentage of squirrel keratinocytes responded to cold with larger calcium transients (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The average cold threshold in human keratinocyte samples was ~19°C.
source: The average cold threshold in our human samples was ~19°C; in previous studies, cold thresholds were not reported, but peak cold responses were observed between 16–18°C (Tsutsumi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data from the experiments described.

claim: In previous studies, cold thresholds in human keratinocytes were not reported, but peak cold responses were observed between 16–18°C.
source: The average cold threshold in our human samples was ~19°C; in previous studies, cold thresholds were not reported, but peak cold responses were observed between 16–18°C (Tsutsumi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Only 36% of keratinocytes responded to cold when incubated with 20 µM EGTA and 0 µM Ca2+.
source: Under these conditions, only 36% of keratinocytes responded to cold (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Cells that responded to cold in the absence of extracellular calcium exhibited smaller calcium transients (25% decrease from vehicle).
source: cells that did respond exhibited smaller calcium transients (25% decrease from vehicle; Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Cells that responded to cold in the absence of extracellular calcium responded at lower temperatures (0.6°C decrease from vehicle).
source: and responded at lower temperatures (0.6°C decrease from vehicle; Figure 2D) than vehicle-exposed cells.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Removal of extracellular sodium (equimolar NMDG substitution) had no additional effect on keratinocyte cold responses.
source: Removal of extracellular sodium (equimolar NMDG substitution) had no additional effect on keratinocyte cold responses, therefore arguing against cold-sensitive sodium channels (e.g. epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) [Askwith et al., 2001]) being the primary cold detectors.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data from the experiments described.

claim: Keratinocyte cold responses were only completely eliminated when the extracellular buffer included 20 µM EGTA and 0 µM Ca2+ and intracellular calcium stores were depleted with 1 µM thapsigargin immediately prior to the cold ramp.
source: Keratinocyte cold responses were only completely eliminated when the extracellular buffer included 20 µM EGTA and 0 µM Ca2+ and intracellular calcium stores were depleted with 1 µM thapsigargin immediately prior to the cold ramp (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: STIM/Orai CRAC channels are required for normal warming and 'heat-off' responses in human and mouse keratinocytes.
source: While not a member of the TRP superfamily, the STIM/Orai CRAC channels are required for normal warming and 'heat-off' responses in human and mouse keratinocytes (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Incubation with 5J4 did not change the percentage of keratinocytes responding to cold.
source: However, incubation with 5J4 did not change the percentage of keratinocytes responding to cold (Figure 2B) or the magnitude of the peak cold response (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Incubation with 5J4 did not change the magnitude of the peak cold response.
source: However, incubation with 5J4 did not change the percentage of keratinocytes responding to cold (Figure 2B) or the magnitude of the peak cold response (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Extracellular application of 5J4 lowered the average cold threshold by 0.4°C.
source: Extracellular application of 5J4 did lower the average cold threshold by 0.4°C, but the biological significance of this decreases is unclear (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Bidaux et al. identified a novel epidermal isoform of the cold and menthol-sensitive channel TRPM8 (eTRPM8) in the endoplasmic reticulum of human keratinocytes.
source: Bidaux et al. identified a novel epidermal isoform of the cold and menthol-sensitive (McKemy et al., 2002; Peier et al., 2002a) channel TRPM8 (eTRPM8) in the endoplasmic reticulum of human keratinocytes (Bidaux et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: TRPM8 is a cold and menthol-sensitive channel.
source: Bidaux et al. identified a novel epidermal isoform of the cold and menthol-sensitive (McKemy et al., 2002; Peier et al., 2002a) channel TRPM8 (eTRPM8) in the endoplasmic reticulum of human keratinocytes (Bidaux et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Only 1 of the 460 mouse keratinocytes tested responded to menthol.
source: However unlike Bidaux et al., 2015, we did not observe menthol-induced calcium transients in mouse keratinocytes (Figure 2B). Given that Biduax et al. performed their experiments in conditions that reduced capacitive calcium flux (i.e. reduced CRAC channel activity), we expected to observe even larger menthol responses in our experiments, but only 1 of the 460 mouse keratinocytes tested responded to menthol
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data from the experiments described.

claim: The percentage of cold-sensitive cells and peak cold responses in TRPA1 knockout keratinocytes were similar to those observed in wildtype keratinocytes.
source: In mouse, the percentage of cold-sensitive cells and peak cold responses in TRPA1 knockout keratinocytes were similar to those observed in wildtype keratinocytes (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 2B and C.

claim: TRPA1 knockout keratinocytes exhibited cold-induced calcium transients at warmer temperatures than wildtype keratinocytes (21.5°C vs. 20.9°C).
source: On average, TRPA1 knockout keratinocytes exhibited cold-induced calcium transients at warmer temperatures than wildtype keratinocytes (21.5°C vs. 20.9°C; Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: TRPA1 is a member of the TRP ion channel superfamily involved in detection of noxious cold (<17°C).
source: TRPA1 is a member of the TRP ion channel superfamily involved in detection of noxious cold (<17°C) (Story et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Extracellular application of the TRPA1 antagonist HC-030031 partially decreases cold-induced calcium transients in human keratinocytes.
source: In human keratinocyte studies, extracellular application of the TRPA1 antagonist HC-030031 partially decreases cold-induced calcium transients (Tsutsumi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: TRPA1 expression or function has not been verified in mouse epidermal cells.
source: This lack of TRPA1 involvement was not surprising as we and others have not been able to verify TRPA1 expression or function in mouse epidermal cells (Bouvier et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2013; Zappia et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Global TRPA1 knockout mice exhibit normal cold-induced reflexive behaviors.
source: Additionally, global TRPA1 knockout mice (Bautista et al., 2006) and rats (Reese et al., 2020) exhibit normal cold-induced reflexive behaviors, further suggesting that this channel is not a conserved noxious cold transducer in mammalian skin cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Global TRPA1 knockout rats exhibit normal cold-induced reflexive behaviors.
source: Additionally, global TRPA1 knockout mice (Bautista et al., 2006) and rats (Reese et al., 2020) exhibit normal cold-induced reflexive behaviors, further suggesting that this channel is not a conserved noxious cold transducer in mammalian skin cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: TRPC5 is a cold-sensitive TRP channel family member expressed in keratinocytes.
source: TRPC5 is another cold-sensitive TRP channel family member (Zimmermann et al., 2011) expressed in keratinocytes (Beck et al., 2006) that could be a plasma membrane-expressed cold sensor.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: TRPC5 knockout keratinocyte cold responses were identical to those observed in wildtype tissue.
source: TRPC5 knockout keratinocyte cold responses were identical to those observed in wildtype tissue (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data presented in Figure 2.

claim: When expressed in heterologous cells, TRPC5 currents peak around 25°C.
source: This result may be related to the temperatures used in this experiment; when expressed in heterologous cells, TRPC5 currents peak around 25°C (Zimmermann et al., 2011), the starting temperature of our experiments.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Global TRPC5 knockout mice exhibit normal cold behavioral responses.
source: Alternatively, TRPC5 activity may not be required for normal cold sensation; global TRPC5 knockout mice exhibit normal cold behavioral responses (Zimmermann et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: There is at least one intracellular cold-sensitive protein that is required for keratinocyte cold activity.
source: Based on our characterization studies however, there is at least one intracellular cold-sensitive protein that is required for keratinocyte cold activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that cold responses require intracellular calcium release.

claim: Krt14:Arch Cre+ mice exhibited longer withdrawal latencies to the dry ice stimulus when 590 nm light was applied to the stimulated hindpaw.
source: Krt14:Arch Cre+ mice exhibited longer withdrawal latencies to the dry ice stimulus when 590 nm light was applied to the stimulated hindpaw (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Keratinocyte activity contributes to normal cold sensation and behavioral responses in vivo.
source: Based on these data, keratinocyte activity contributes to normal cold sensation and behavioral responses in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the optogenetic inhibition experiments showing increased withdrawal latencies.

claim: Keratinocytes release ATP when mechanically stimulated.
source: We and others have shown that keratinocytes release ATP when mechanically stimulated (Klusch et al., 2013; Koizumi et al., 2004; Moehring et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: ATP released from keratinocytes can bind to P2X4 receptors expressed in Aβ, Aδ, and C fiber afferents, effectively depolarizing neuronal membranes and increasing the likelihood of fiber firing.
source: This ATP can subsequently bind to members of the P2Y receptor family or, as demonstrated in our previous publication, P2X4 receptors expressed in Aβ, Aδ, and C fiber afferents, effectively depolarizing neuronal membranes and increasing the likelihood of fiber firing (Koizumi et al., 2004; Moehring et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Apyrase-injected animals exhibited longer withdrawal latencies to the dry ice stimulus than vehicle-injected controls.
source: Apyrase-injected animals exhibited longer withdrawal latencies to the dry ice stimulus than vehicle-injected controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: P2X4cKO mice exhibited longer withdrawal latencies to dry ice stimulation than control littermates.
source: We also tested the cold sensitivity of sensory neuron-specific P2X4 knockout mice (P2X4cKO; AdvilCre::P2rX4 fl/fl). P2X4cKO mice exhibited longer withdrawal latencies to dry ice stimulation than control littermates (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Control mice displayed a place preference for the 30°C floor when it was paired with floors held at 23, 20, and 17°C.
source: Control mice displayed a place preference for the 30°C floor when it was paired with floors held at 23, 20, and 17°C; P2X4cKO mice spent more time on these colder floors than controls (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: P2X4cKO mice spent more time on colder floors (23, 20, and 17°C) than controls in a two-temperature preference test.
source: Control mice displayed a place preference for the 30°C floor when it was paired with floors held at 23, 20, and 17°C; P2X4cKO mice spent more time on these colder floors than controls (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: ATP-P2X4 signaling mediates normal cold sensation in vivo.
source: Collectively, these findings are similar to those observed in mechanosensory tests and suggest that ATP-P2X4 signaling also mediates normal cold sensation in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral experiments with apyrase and P2X4cKO mice.

claim: The noxious heat receptor TRPV1 was visualized in human keratinocytes.
source: Since the noxious heat receptor TRPV1 was visualized in human keratinocytes (Denda et al., 2001), many have hypothesized that these non-neuronal cells are involved in thermosensation (Chung et al., 2004; Dhaka et al., 2006; Lee and Caterina, 2005; Moqrich, 2005; Peier et al., 2002b).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Primary human and mouse keratinocytes exhibit heat-evoked currents.
source: Primary human and mouse keratinocytes exhibit heat-evoked currents (Chung et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2019; Tsutsumi et al., 2011) and release ATP upon warming (Mandadi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Keratinocytes release ATP upon warming.
source: Primary human and mouse keratinocytes exhibit heat-evoked currents (Chung et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2019; Tsutsumi et al., 2011) and release ATP upon warming (Mandadi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Heat responses in keratinocytes are reportedly mediated by TRPV3, TRPV4, and STIM1/Orai channels.
source: These heat responses are reportedly mediated by TRPV3 (Moqrich, 2005), TRPV4 (Chung et al., 2004), and STIM1/Orai channels (Liu et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Global TRPV3/TRPV4 double knockout mice exhibit normal behavioral responses to innocuous and noxious heat stimulation.
source: but global TPRV3/TRPV4 double knockout mice exhibit normal behavioral responses to innocuous and noxious heat stimulation (Huang et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Keratinocytes isolated from TRPV3/TRPV4 double knockout mice exhibit heat responses identical to those observed in wildtype tissues.
source: and keratinocytes isolated from these animals exhibit heat responses identical to those observed in wildtype tissues (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Capsaicin responses have not been observed in primary mouse keratinocytes.
source: Furthermore, we and others have not observed capsaicin responses in primary mouse keratinocytes (Chung et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work and the authors' own observations.

claim: Keratinocytes may express a complement of functionally redundant proteins that compensate for reduced activity of related temperature-sensitive channels.
source: Similar to sensory neurons (Vandewauw et al., 2018), keratinocytes may express a complement of functionally redundant proteins that compensate for reduced activity of related temperature-sensitive channels.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on analogy to sensory neurons.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of keratin14-expressing cells decreased activity in heat-sensitive polymodal C and Aδ nociceptors.
source: Baumbauer, DeBerry, and Adelman et al. previously demonstrated that keratinocyte activity contributes to ex vivo peripheral thermal transduction processes; optogenetic inhibition of keratin14-expressing cells decreased activity in heat-sensitive polymodal C and Aδ nociceptors (Baumbauer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Krt14:Arch Cre+ mice exhibited longer withdrawal latencies to the heat stimulus when 590 nm light was applied to the stimulated hindpaw.
source: Krt14:Arch Cre+ mice exhibited longer withdrawal latencies to the heat stimulus when 590 nm light was applied to the stimulated hindpaw (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Wildtype animals injected with apyrase exhibited longer withdrawal latencies to the heat stimulus when compared to controls.
source: Wildtype animals injected with apyrase and P2X4cKO mice also exhibited longer withdrawal latencies to the heat stimulus when compared to the appropriate controls (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: P2X4cKO mice exhibited longer withdrawal latencies to the heat stimulus when compared to controls.
source: Wildtype animals injected with apyrase and P2X4cKO mice also exhibited longer withdrawal latencies to the heat stimulus when compared to the appropriate controls (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: These data are the first to demonstrate the conserved requirement of keratinocyte activity for normal mechanical, cold, and heat sensation in vivo.
source: Collectively, these and our previous data (Moehring et al., 2018) are the first to demonstrate the conserved requirement of keratinocyte activity for normal mechanical, cold, and heat sensation in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current and previous experimental data.

claim: Primary sensory neurons are capable of detecting and encoding environmental stimuli without accessory cells.
source: While it is true that primary sensory neurons are capable of detecting and encoding environmental stimuli without accessory cells, our work suggests that proper somatosensation also requires critical stimulus amplification at the level of the keratinocyte.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Proper somatosensation requires critical stimulus amplification at the level of the keratinocyte.
source: While it is true that primary sensory neurons are capable of detecting and encoding environmental stimuli without accessory cells, our work suggests that proper somatosensation also requires critical stimulus amplification at the level of the keratinocyte.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that keratinocyte inhibition reduces sensory responses.

claim: Keratinocyte population activity could explain the extreme variability observed in DRG cold responses in vivo.
source: Keratinocyte population activity (Koizumi et al., 2004) could also explain the extreme variability observed in DRG cold responses in vivo (Luiz et al., 2019; individual sensory neuron activity could be directly influenced by the non-neuronal cells in the local peripheral terminal environment.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Global chemo- and optogenetic approaches had been used to illustrate the importance of keratinocyte-to-sensory neuron signaling in somatosensation before this work.
source: Before our work, global chemo- (Pang et al., 2015) and optogenetic (Baumbauer et al., 2015; Moehring et al., 2018) approaches had been used to illustrate the importance of keratinocyte-to-sensory neuron signaling in somatosensation.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Non-specific keratinocyte activation methods did not allow for the interrogation of specific sensory modalities as generic keratinocyte activation quickly induced nocifensive and paresthesia-like behaviors in mice.
source: However, these non-specific activation methods did not allow for the interrogation of specific sensory modalities as generic keratinocyte activation quickly induced nocifensive and paresthesia-like behaviors in mice (Baumbauer et al., 2015; Moehring et al., 2018; Pang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Epidermal purinergic signaling is a ubiquitous but critical mechanism that amplifies many modalities of somatosensory stimuli.
source: These and our former studies (Moehring et al., 2018) also position epidermal purinergic signaling as a ubiquitous but critical mechanism that amplifies many modalities of somatosensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current and previous experimental data.

claim: All cold-responsive keratinocytes exhibited sustained calcium transients that began during the initial dynamic phase of the cold ramp and ended during the static cold hold phase.
source: All cold-responsive keratinocytes exhibited sustained calcium transients that began during the initial dynamic phase of the cold ramp and ended during the static cold hold phase.
evidence: This is a description of the observed calcium imaging data.

claim: Cytosolic calcium levels began to decrease during the static phase of the temperature ramp.
source: Cytosolic calcium levels began to decrease during the static phase of the temperature ramp, and a second increase in cytosolic calcium was not observed during re-warming.
evidence: This is a description of the observed calcium imaging data.

claim: A second increase in cytosolic calcium was not observed during re-warming.
source: Cytosolic calcium levels began to decrease during the static phase of the temperature ramp, and a second increase in cytosolic calcium was not observed during re-warming.
evidence: This is a description of the observed calcium imaging data.

claim: A warming response was observed in <1% of mouse keratinocytes.
source: If keratinocytes quickly reset their set-point at the temperature nadir (~12°C), we would have expected warming responses to occur during the second dynamic phase of the ramp. However, we observed such a warming response in <1% of mouse keratinocytes.
evidence: This is a description of the observed calcium imaging data.

claim: The cold plantar assay is a preferred measure of cold sensitivity because behavioral responses are highly reproducible and easy to quantify.
source: The cold plantar assay is our preferred measure of cold sensitivity since behavioral responses are highly reproducible and easy to quantify.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological choice made by the authors.

claim: The nature of the dry ice stimulus elicits anticipatory cold-related behaviors rather than pain-related behaviors elicited by discrete noxious cold temperatures.
source: The nature of the dry ice stimulus elicits anticipatory cold-related behaviors rather than pain-related behaviors elicited by discrete noxious cold temperatures.
